newsitem.title: GERMANY: German failure to enter EMU would send mark up.
newsitem.headline: German failure to enter EMU would send mark up.

text.p: German Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said on Thursday that the failure by Germany to enter European monetary union would cause the mark to rise sharply.
"If a decision was reached that Germany does not participate from the start we'd get a sharp rise in the mark," Kuehbacher told journalists in Hamburg.
He also said that German tax hikes could allow Bonn to meet the EMU criteria exactly.

Speaking generally about EMU, Kuebacher further noted that any stability pact would have to have automatic sanctions for it to succeed and that it remained to be seen whether Italy would succeed in meeting the EMU criteria.
On the possibility of German tax increases being used to ease Germany's way towards the EMU entry criteria, Kuehbacher noted:

"If the finance minister and the government came to the conclusion that Europe is more important than the coalition's promise not to raise taxes then that would be a door to reaching an exact meeting of the criteria," Kuehbacher said.

He said that he saw a general movement away from a "numerical assessment" of adherence to the Maastrict criteria and that this meant a stability pact post-EMU was becoming more important as a means to insure a credible Euro.
"A stability pact without automatic, self-triggering sanctions is not a proper stability pact," Kuehbacher said.
Asked about Italy's performance on the road to EMU, Kuehbacher said: "We will all have to wait and see whether the Italian government succeeds in its effort to create the conditions required.
"They entail brutal budget cuts and we will have to see whether the population goes along with them. After all governments have to fight elections," he said.
Referring to Germany, Kuehbacher said the budget deficit to GDP ratio was more likely to be at 3.6 percent in 1996 than at 3.0 percent -- the reference level laid down in the Maastricht treaty.
